props.title: The Tin Star
props.initialSlug: Outlaws' last stand at the Tin Star.

sections.content: **The Tin Star** (1957) stands as a masterful Western that helped define the mentor-protégé relationship in law enforcement films. Anthony Mann directs Henry Fonda as an experienced bounty hunter teaching Anthony Perkins' rookie sheriff, creating a template that influenced everything from **Training Day** (2001) to **Unforgiven** (1992). The film's stark black-and-white cinematography by Loyal Griggs captures the moral absolutes of frontier justice while suggesting deeper shades of gray in its characters' motivations.

sections.content: Mann's direction in **The Tin Star** showcases his signature approach to psychological Westerns, a style he perfected in films like **Winchester '73** (1950) and **The Naked Spur** (1953). The film explores how law and morality intersect through Fonda's cynical ex-lawman Morg Hickman, whose tragic past shapes his complex relationship with authority. This theme of the disillusioned lawman would later influence films like **Open Range** (2003) and **Appaloosa** (2008).

The film's treatment of racial prejudice through the subplot involving Kip Mayfield and his Native American wife remains groundbreaking for 1957. This progressive element anticipates later Westerns like **Dances with Wolves** (1990) and **Little Big Man** (1970), which would more directly confront the genre's traditional portrayal of Native Americans. sections.content: Fonda's performance as Morg Hickman established a template for the weathered lawman passing on his knowledge that would influence countless Westerns. This archetype appears in **Tombstone** (1993) with Val Kilmer's Doc Holliday guiding Kurt Russell's Wyatt Earp, and even in modern crime films like **No Country for Old Men** (2007), where Tommy Lee Jones' sheriff represents the old guard of law enforcement facing a changing world.
